At least nine AI Developer Platforms have disclosed incidents over the course of the month:

- Fireworks AI (Oct 6)

- Andromeda (Oct 9)

- Zeabur (Oct 14)

- Lightning AI (Oct 15)

- OpenCode (Oct 16–17)

- Railway (Oct 20)

- Warp (Oct 23)

- CommandCode (Oct 28)

- Northflank (Oct 30)

Wiz customers can refer to our relevant Threat Intel Center advisories for more information on the Railway Platform Breach, Lightning AI Security Incident and the overall campaign .

Fireworks , OpenCode , and Warp have all reported indications of an “agent swarm” attack. Andromeda’s incident report calls it part of an "industry-wide attack." OpenCode and CommandCode have explicitly attributed their incidents to an attempt at “ distillation .”

Any other month, and this would be the top security story. However, with all the ongoing incidents, few reports are connecting the dots across these attacks (Cloud Security Alliance as a notable exception ).

## The Pattern in these Attacks

Currently, most of these security incidents are still being analyzed, and detailed technical information is not available. Zeabur has shared a full write-up, and the company will be shutting down due to this incident. Railway has released a preliminary report and timeline .

However, there are some indicative details. Fireworks, Zeabur, and Lightning all attribute their incident root causes to credential access. Lightning was previously impacted by a supply chain attack within the Mini-Shai Hulud campaign . Railway so far has shared they believe the initial access was via “privilege escalation in our build infrastructure,” while Warp has suggested the root cause was a third-party vendor dependency, and OpenCode attributes it to a “legacy system.”

All public reports highlight targeted exploitation, explicitly hunting stored environment variables, with a focus on those granting AI access. While there is no single vulnerability or dependency linking these attacks, the overall picture is strongly aligned with recent reports on two fronts:

Agentic Attacks , which can enable threat actors to compromise victims faster and more efficiently.

The rise of LLMJacking , and the associated infrastructure of LLM Brokers. These create a market that makes the theft easily monetizable, likely driving more actors to undertake operations to steal credentials. Distillation , notably alleged against Chinese AI labs, drives demand as well.

## Impact and Follow-on activity

Reports on the impact of these attacks have so far been limited to anecdotal reports on social media, which include:

- Alleged theft of cryptocurrency, to the tune of ~$371,000 , using crypto keys stored in Railway

- Abuse of stolen AI access, such as those from OpenCode, resulting in consumer bills in the hundreds to thousands of dollars

However, Wiz has been able to observe downstream abuse of enterprise credentials , whose compromise we can attribute to one of these vendor breaches. We will discuss an exemplary pair of such cases.

In both cases, we see abuse of keys that previously were heavily used from the infrastructure of a compromised vendor.

They shared an identical first unauthorized activity, which happened within 30 minutes of the reported credential access within the vendor breach. It was a single InvokeModel from a residential IP address, in a one-minute sweep that tested stolen keys across multiple organizations. The call asked for Claude Fable 5.1, failed, and fell back to Opus 5.5, which worked.

In the days after this initial validation, both keys saw only a trickle of traffic: 14–120 calls a day from the same small Go client. The calls on the two keys ran in lockstep, about a minute apart. This indicates a single ongoing verification job checking that the keys remained valid.

### Case A

Four days after the initial validation, a rotating proxy pool ran a catalog probe across dozens of addresses, sending one call per model across vendors: Amazon Nova, DeepSeek, gpt-oss, GLM, Kimi, Grok, GPT-6 Astra and older Claude models. Every call worked except Fable. A few hours later, a boto3 script on a residential address enumerated Bedrock and EC2 quotas. Twenty-two seconds after that, bulk traffic started from the same address. Within the next half hour, a second host mapped quotas and model availability across regions, making more than a thousand calls in under a minute.

The Flood

Over thirty hours, after which the key was remediated, the actor made approximately 800k Bedrock calls, and about 90% of them succeeded. The bulk ran first from the residential address and then, overnight, from a Level 3 hosting address. The key's policy allowed global.* cross-region inference profiles, and the actor routed every call through them. Because global routing spread the load across regions, only about 6% of calls were throttled. Traffic leaned heavily on Opus: Opus models were three quarters of successful calls, led by Opus 5 (36%), Opus 5.5 (22%) and Opus 4.8 (10%).

### Case B

Unlike Case A, this key was restricted. Seven days after the initial validation, it surfaced in an apparent reseller pool. Over four hours, thousands of failed calls came from rotating hosting addresses, each active for about 15 minutes. The calls failed because the key's policy allowed Bedrock only through us.* cross-region inference profiles, and the pool requested global.* .

Early the next morning, a checker on a shared VPN exit identified the working us.* model IDs. Two hours later, a boto3 script on a Level 3 address retested global.* and us.* and enumerated Bedrock and EC2 quotas. It was the same script, down to the version string, that had probed Case A. Within minutes, the floodgates opened.

Over thirteen hours, after which the key was remediated, that single Level 3 address made approximately 1.7 million Bedrock calls, with over a million successful. Nearly all of the rest were throttled: without global routing, the traffic ran into the account's regional quotas. Traffic was spread across a dozen Claude models and was less Opus-heavy than Case A. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 5 made up three quarters of successful calls.

### The Stolen Tokens

In both cases, the token usage profile resembles resold coding-agent traffic. A typical call sent only a handful of uncached input tokens, the signature of prompt caching, and got back a few hundred tokens of output. A long tail of calls carried tens of thousands of uncached input tokens, consistent with many different end users behind a reseller. At list price, these two cases alone likely ran up over $100k in usage .

## What we see from these Attackers

Our research has been able to link the usage of the keys in the cases above overt reselling organizations. While we are not able to definitively establish the relationship between these reselling organizations and either the initial compromise or the “flood” token abuse documented above, the actors had access to the compromised keys and tested them from their infrastructure. The use of the keys by multiple actors suggests a robust market for this type of credential.

### “momo” - Resale (and compromise?)

Wiz Research identified an actor centered around 23.106.46.239 who appears to refer to themselves as “momo” who had access to the keys used in Case A and Case B and is tied to an overt LLM resale site. Infrastructure linked to this IP address goes back to 2025 and has hosted multiple sites with titles related to LLM resale, including the site llm-routing.com which is currently active and advertises discounted access to frontier models, while accepting payment in USDT. This IP has also hosted an Artex landing page in mid-October and was publicly named by Zeabur as being part of their compromise. While we cannot definitively tie this operation to the “flood” of abuse documented above, the operator did have access to the stolen keys.

- The site momo.skin resolved to 23.106.46.239 in early 2026 and another site tied via passive dns ( direct.465415.xyz ), used the title "Moの自建网盘" ("Mo's self-built cloud drive").

- In March of 2026, this actor begins advertising LLM related services, hosting sites with titles such as "ChatGPT Team 席位兑换" ("ChatGPT Team seat redemption"), and "ChatGPT 号池管理" ("ChatGPT account-pool management").

- On October 8, 2026, a subdomain ( artex.nhhh.de ) resolving to 23.106.46.239 hosted a page with the title “ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台" ("ARTEX — autonomous penetration testing console"). This is four days before Zeabur’s timeline identifying that IP address targeting their infrastructure (Oct 12 - 14).

- In late October the 23.106.46.239 address conducts api key checks on the keys used in cases A and B and attempts a PutAccountDataRetention call using the Case B key.

### “Xingjiabi” - a second resale hub

Wiz also identified a second resale operation that was leveraging stolen keys. This one is publicly available at xingjiabiapi.org where they offer access to a wide range of frontier models for discount prices. Infrastructure tied to this site ( 38.246.114.118 ) was identified conducting permission checks on the keys used in both cases A and B. In both cases the checks were conducted after the high volume abuse of the key from unrelated ip addresses had already begun, suggesting that there is an active resale market for these keys.

- A subdomain of the main site, s3.xingjiabiapi.org resolved to 38.246.114.118 beginning on September 10, 2026. This 38.246.114.118 IP address enumerated the key used in case A, listing the inference profiles and models per region, paging through every bedrock quota. It also conducted a manual test of the key being used in Case B.

- One interesting note about this actor is they seem to be attempting to guard against distillation. Their domain was snapshotted hosting a page titled “蒸馏检测监控” (Distillation behaviour detection) that was designed to score users across three categories and attempt to sort them into “high risk”, “watch” and “normal”. This may indicate that the attackers are attempting to avoid being associated with distillation, potentially due to that activity leading to accounts being suspended.

# Executive Summary

- Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them.

- PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others.

- These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it , putting every affected website in immediate risk.

- Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.

- On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine.

- These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.

# Overview

In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure.

Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.

PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure.

Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging. Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

Wiz Research would like to thank the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI for their work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. OpenAI and Calif also published blogs containing details on the vulnerability – its history, technical details, and insight into the disclosure process. PHP posted as well.

We’d also like to express our sincere gratitude towards Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare , Fastly, Google , Imperva, Microsoft, Vercel, and many others, for helping prepare guidance and out-of-the-box mitigations for customers who cannot apply the patch immediately.

# The Vulnerabilities

All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.

While this blog covers only four instances of exploitable bugs (grouped under two CVEs) that follow this problematic pattern, there are other tracked, and likely untracked, variants of this issue in the PHP codebase. These variants have different requirements for exploitation and can lead to different types of impact. In any case, the patch provided by the PHP team fixes the issue at its core and eliminates all variants in the patched release.

# Impact

We combined these vulnerabilities into a single exploit script, php2shell, and demonstrated that it could execute code remotely without authentication on deployments of WordPress ( wordpress:latest ), Drupal ( drupal:latest ), and Joomla ( joomla:latest ), using their latest container images at the time of testing.

These platforms illustrate the impact, but the vulnerabilities are in PHP itself. Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.

Separately, we demonstrated that attackers could read sensitive data from the PHP process’s memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys, without needing to achieve remote code execution.

# The AI inflection point

The vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade. Turning these flaws into working exploits required chaining multiple bugs and accounting for how PHP allocates and reuses memory across requests. Memory bugs are notoriously complex; differences in PHP versions, configurations and application behavior can break assumptions the exploit depends on. An attack that works against one deployment may need substantial adjustments to work against another, each requiring further analysis, testing and debugging. Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale.

With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts. With testing and debugging tools, models can analyze failures and iterate on adjustments, reducing the specialist effort required for each target. This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. As AI reduces the effort needed to develop and adapt complex exploits, vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets.

We used Wiz Atlas , Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research. Notably, Gemini 4 Argon made an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.

# Industry-level collaborations

Prior to public disclosure, Wiz Research worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI on discovery, coordination and patch verification. We also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, AWS, Microsoft, Automattic, Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, Vercel and many others to prepare customer guidance, detections and out-of-the-box mitigations for organizations that cannot update immediately.

Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.

# Technical deep dive

## Bug: Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

PHP's Session module can decode session data during upload-progress handling in the same pre-initialization window. The decoder stores request-owned bookkeeping in BG(unserialize) . A fatal allocation failure can interrupt this path, destroy the request heap and leave the unserializer's global state published.

On a later request handled by the same worker, PHP can consume attacker-reclaimed memory as live unserializer bookkeeping. The stale state becomes a powerful memory-corruption primitive. We combined it with the memory disclosure to remove address uncertainty and achieved unauthenticated remote code execution on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.

The WordPress, Drupal and Joomla chains are representative demonstrations. The underlying primitives exist at the PHP engine level and can affect any PHP application running on a vulnerable version.

These issues execute below the application layer, so application logs may contain little context. Until systems are patched, defenders should pay particular attention to unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained PHP worker churn. These signals can guide an investigation. Applying the PHP security update remains the only complete remediation.

## Bug: Remote process-memory disclosure

PHP parses RFC1867 multipart requests during request startup, before normal module initialization has completed. Session upload-progress handling can initialize Session state at this early stage and publish a session ID in PS(id) . An out-of-memory error can abort the request before cleanup completes. PHP then destroys the request heap and may leave PS(id) pointing to the freed allocation.

A later multipart request handled by the same worker can reach the upload-progress cleanup path before normal Session initialization resets that pointer. PHP trusts the stale pointer and length as a live zend_string and URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The attack works even when the application never calls session_start() , making the issue application-agnostic. We demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of an attacker-sized region of live worker memory containing data from outside the attacker's request.
